newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: World airlines report lower profits in 1996.
newsitem.headline: World airlines report lower profits in 1996.

text.p: Net profits of international airlines fell to $4 billion in 1996 from a record $5.2 billion in 1995 because of fare cuts and higher-than-expected fuel costs, the world airline body IATA said on Wednesday.

Pierre Jeanniot, director-general of the International Air Transport Association, said profits in 1997 were forecast to rise only slightly to $4.4 billion, below 1995's record, and urged airlines to economise.
"We are certainly back with half a loaf," Jeanniot said in a statement.
"It's easy to buy airplanes. It's harder but perhaps smarter not to buy airplanes. At the very least, airline chief executives should insist on modernising and not just expanding their fleets."
IATA's 254 member airlines reported total revenues of $134.3 billion in 1996 against operating costs of $127.2 billion and interest charges of $3 billion.
International airlines have swung back into the black after a recession in the early 1990s when they notched up total losses of $15.2 billion.
In 1996, net airline profits were less than three percent of revenues and average yield was down by 2.5 percent -- more than a one percent fall in unit cost.
Fuel accounted for 12 percent of the operating costs of IATA members and charges for airport use and traffic control services made up another 10 percent of the costs.
Airline capacity expanding faster than the growth in international air traffic was one reason behind the decline in 1996's profits, IATA said.
This gap was expected to widen in 1997 with traffic forecast to expand by seven percent and capacity by 7.5 pct, it said.
